# Esther Chapter 7 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 458r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_007_page_001.jpg

---

**1** So the king and Haman went to Queen Esther's banquet. **2** As they were drinking wine on this second day, the king asked Esther again, "Tell me what you want, Queen Esther — it will be yours. What is your request? I would give you up to half my kingdom."

**3** Queen Esther replied, "Your Majesty, if you are pleased with me, and if it seems right to the king — I ask for my life. That is my petition. And I ask for the lives of my people. That is my request. **4** For my people and I have been sold to destruction — to slaughter and annihilation. If we had only been sold into slavery, I would have held my tongue; that hardship would not be worth bothering the king about. But this is extermination."

**5** King Ahasuerus demanded of Queen Esther, "Who is this person? Where is the man who has dared to do this?" **6** Esther answered, "Our adversary and enemy — is this vile man, Haman!" Haman froze in terror before the king and queen.

**7** The king stormed out in a rage from the banquet into the palace garden. Haman, realizing the king had already decided his fate, stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life. **8** When the king returned from the garden to the banquet hall, he found Haman collapsed on the couch where Esther was reclining. "Is he going to assault the queen right here in my palace?" the king roared. The moment the words left the king's mouth, attendants covered Haman's face.

**9** Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs serving the king, spoke up: "There is also the matter of the gallows — seventy-five feet tall — standing at Haman's house. He built it for Mordecai, the man who saved Your Majesty's life." "Hang him on it," said the king. **10** So they hanged Haman on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai, and the king's rage subsided.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Esther's moment of disclosure:** This is the scene toward which the entire book has been building. Esther finally reveals her identity and her people's peril in a single devastating sentence. The Hebrew author structures Esther's speech with rising tension: first the abstract legal language of being "sold" (*nimkarnu*), then the escalating triad — "destroyed, killed, annihilated" — the same three verbs from Haman's original decree (3:13). By echoing Haman's own language, Esther forces the king to hear his own edict through the ears of its victims.

**The gallows that backfire:** The book of Esther is built on reversals (*peripeteia*), and the gallows are the supreme symbol. Built by Haman for Mordecai, they become the instrument of Haman's own death. The Hebrew word *ets* (tree/wood) carries echoes of the "tree of knowledge" — the instrument of downfall always turns on the one who wields it in arrogance.

*— PNEUMA*
